Systemic inflammation

Human and mouse studies found changes in selected cytokines, with some reductions and some increases depending on baseline or marker. A related periodontal study reported lower serum IL-6 after local PBM, but no study established improvement in symptoms or disease outcomes.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Human and mouse studies found changes in selected cytokines, with some reductions and some increases depending on baseline or marker. A related periodontal study reported lower serum IL-6 after local PBM, but no study established improvement in symptoms or disease outcomes.

Summary of the Evidence

Two publications are directly classified as systemic-inflammation studies: a sham-controlled human cytokine experiment and a mouse surgical-inflammation experiment. A third, narrowly mapped study measured serum IL-6 after local gingival PBM in people with periodontitis and type 2 diabetes; it did not test systemic light delivery. Direct blood irradiation was an ex-vivo component of the same human publication, not a separate cohort. These papers measure cytokines rather than clinical recovery from an inflammatory disease.

Human and clinical evidence

In a randomized, placebo-controlled study of 62 volunteers, broad-spectrum polarized visible and infrared light was applied over the sacral area. In participants whose starting levels were elevated, TNF-α, IL-6, and IFN-γ fell soon after exposure; reductions in TNF-α and IL-6 persisted after repeated treatments. Some anti-inflammatory markers rose when their initial levels were low. IFN-γ also rose in participants whose baseline values were normal, while several other cytokines did not change. Thus, the response was marker- and baseline-dependent rather than a uniform decrease in inflammation (Zhevago and Samoilova 2006).

The mapped periodontal study reported lower serum IL-6 after local 660-nm red-light treatment added to periodontal care, at six weeks and three months. Because light was applied to the gums and the population had periodontitis with diabetes, this is related evidence about a possible systemic biomarker response, not a trial of systemic PBM (Mrasori et al. 2021).

Animal evidence

In a 50-mouse surgical-inflammation experiment, 780-nm near-infrared laser treatment decreased TNF-α and IFN-γ released by spleen mononuclear cells, particularly after two sessions. It did not change IL-6 or TGF-β1. This marker-specific response is consistent with the human study showing that not all cytokines move in the same direction (Fukuda et al. 2013).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

The human study also irradiated blood samples directly at 2.4 J/cm². Some cytokine patterns resembled those seen after transcutaneous exposure, but these samples came from the same volunteers and do not add a separate human treatment cohort.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The human experiment used polarized light spanning 480–3400 nm, from visible light into near-infrared, at 12 J/cm² transcutaneously and 2.4 J/cm² for blood samples, over five daily 300-second exposures. The mouse experiment used 780-nm near-infrared light at 10 J/cm² and 20 mW, with three points per session and one to three sessions. The mapped periodontal report used local 660-nm red light. These protocols and targets are not interchangeable, and no clinical dose comparison was reported.

Interpretation

The studies show that selected cytokines can change after light exposure, but the pattern varies by marker and starting level. The available work does not establish that those laboratory changes reduce symptoms, complications, or disease activity in patients.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term changes in selected cytokines after broad-spectrum light exposure Very low for clinical improvement in inflammatory disease
Publications and records3 relevant publications, including one narrow periodontal mapping

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A sham-controlled human study found short-term changes in several blood cytokines, with the direction depending partly on their starting levels. A mouse experiment found lower release of two cytokines, while a related periodontal study used local rather than systemic PBM. These are biomarker findings, not patient benefits. Replicated trials in defined inflammatory conditions are needed.
